strengths: DRE-BO-SSL offers a coherent, potentially useful combination of density-ratio Bayesian optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. Supporting both predefined candidate pools and sampled unlabeled points gives the approach practical flexibility.

The empirical study is substantial: it compares several BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP-based methods across synthetic functions, hyperparameter optimization, architecture search, and an image-based task. Twenty repeated runs with standard errors support the reported improvements, particularly on the synthetic and NATS-Bench experiments.

The paper provides algorithm descriptions, benchmark search spaces, and extensive sensitivity studies covering kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. It also acknowledges computational limitations and the limitations of the cited theory.
weaknesses: The main claimed benefit of unlabeled data is insufficiently isolated. Figure 12 shows that the no-transduction baseline can match or outperform the proposed variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. However, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn beta and obtain substantially different values. Comparable ablations are missing on the application benchmarks, and the random selection heuristic for acquisition plateaus is not separately evaluated. Consequently, the results do not establish how much improvement comes from unlabeled data, kernel bandwidth selection, or acquisition optimization.

The explanation for improved exploration remains largely heuristic. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed inputs does not ensure that high-density regions share the same objective-threshold label, as required by Assumption 4.1. Appendix D asserts that unlabeled points can expand the favorable decision region but does not establish that this occurs or improves optimization. It explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. classification guarantees do not apply to adaptive BO. The qualitative Branin illustrations provide limited evidence for this central mechanism.

Important comparisons and generality checks are missing. The uncertainty-aware DRE work cited in Section 1.1 is particularly relevant to the stated over-exploitation problem, but is not evaluated. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions. The 64D MNIST experiment uses a representation trained to predict the same digit identities that determine the objective, achieving 96.9% test classification accuracy; a baseline that ranks candidates using that pretrained predictor would clarify what additional benefit BO provides.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are unspecified, including the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, input scaling, and bandwidth optimization bounds and initialization. The description also does not clearly explain how continuous L-BFGS-B optimization produces valid candidates in arbitrary finite pools. A smaller, correctable mathematical inconsistency appears before Equation (10): the stated column-normalized definition of P implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text gives P = D^{-1} W; this matters for the transpose used in Equation (11).

Practical computational performance is not adequately established. Dense graph construction, repeated propagation during bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition restarts can incur substantial overhead. Figure 14 studies runtime versus subset size only within the proposed method, with fixed bandwidth; it does not compare total runtime against competitors under the main experimental configuration. Query-efficiency improvements therefore do not establish overall computational advantages.
